result.markdown: # P1 Introduction à R {#sec-r .unnumbered} *Apprentissage préliminaire — bases de R et RStudio* ::: {.callout-warning .translation-pending} ## Traduction en cours Ce chapitre n'a pas encore été traduit : le texte ci-dessous est la version anglaise. ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter, participants should be able to: 1. Use the RStudio interface, create and save scripts, and work within an RStudio Project. 2. Create objects of the principal data types, and select elements of vectors and data frames. 3. Use built-in functions and packages, consult help pages and write simple functions. 4. Import a dataset and manipulate it with the principal `tidyverse` functions. 5. Produce basic graphs with `ggplot2`. 6. Use conditional statements and `for` loops. ::: This chapter introduces the basic elements of the R language. It does not assume previous programming experience. The application of R to the analysis of outbreak data and to modelling is the subject of @sec-r-epi in Module 1, and R is used in the practical sessions of every chapter of the book. Installation instructions are given in @sec-setup. ## P1.1 Interactive tutorials {.unnumbered .keep-short} Participants without previous experience in R are expected to complete the **Applied Epi interactive R tutorials** (sessions 1–6), which are available free of charge in English, French, Portuguese and Spanish at . Each session requires approximately 2–4 hours: | Session | Topic | |---|---| | 1 | Installation of R and RStudio | | 2 | Data preparation | | 3 | R syntax | | 4 | Data cleaning | | 5 | Summary tables | | 6 | Data visualisation with `ggplot2` | | 7 (optional) | Obtaining help and using AI tools | The remainder of this chapter summarises the same material in a compact form, for reference. ## P1.2 RStudio and projects {.unnumbered} RStudio has four panels: the **script editor** (top left), in which code is written and saved; the **console** (bottom left), in which code is executed; the **environment** (top right), which lists the objects in memory; and the **files, plots and help** panel (bottom right). A line of code in a script is executed with *Ctrl + Enter* (*Cmd + Enter* on macOS); text after `#` is a comment and is not executed. Work should be organised in an **RStudio Project** (*File → New Project*). All file paths are then relative to the project folder, so that the analysis can be moved to another computer without modification. ## P1.3 R as a calculator {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} 3 + 4 * 2 # multiplication before addition ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 11 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} (3 + 4) * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 10 / 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 2.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 2^10 # power ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 1024 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sqrt(16) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} exp(1) # the number e ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 2.718282 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} log(100) # natural logarithm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4.60517 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} log10(100) # logarithm with base 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(3.14159, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 3.14 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.4 Objects and assignment {.unnumbered} Values are stored in **objects** with the assignment operator `<-`. Object names are case-sensitive, cannot start with a number, and should be informative. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} population <- 250000 cases <- 375 incidence <- cases / population * 100000 incidence ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 150 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.5 Data types and vectors {.unnumbered} A **vector** is an ordered collection of values of the same type, created with `c()`. The principal types are numeric, character (text), logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`), factor (categorical variable with defined levels) and date. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age <- c(4, 12, 35, 67, 23) # numeric sex <- c("female", "male", "male", "female", "female") # character vaccinated <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE) # logical age_group <- factor(c("0-14", "0-14", "15-64", "65+", "15-64"), levels = c("0-14", "15-64", "65+")) # factor visit <- as.Date(c("2026-03-01", "2026-03-04", "2026-03-04", "2026-03-09", "2026-03-12")) class(age); class(sex); class(vaccinated); class(age_group); class(visit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "logical" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "factor" ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "Date" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} length(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: Arithmetic and comparisons are **vectorised**: they are applied to each element. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age * 12 # age in months ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 48 144 420 804 276 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} age >= 15 # logical vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] FALSE FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(vaccinated) # TRUE counts as 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(vaccinated) # proportion vaccinated ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 0.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} table(age_group) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## age_group ## 0-14 15-64 65+ ## 2 2 1 ``` ::: ::: ### P1.5.1 Selecting elements {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} age[2] # second element ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} age[c(1, 3)] # first and third elements ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4 35 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} age[-1] # all except the first ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 12 35 67 23 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} age[age >= 15] # elements meeting a condition ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 35 67 23 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sex[vaccinated] # sex of vaccinated persons ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "female" "male" "female" ``` ::: ::: ### P1.5.2 Missing values {.unnumbered} Missing values are represented by `NA`. Most summary functions return `NA` if any value is missing, unless `na.rm = TRUE` is specified. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} weight <- c(12.5, NA, 70.2, 64.0, 58.3) mean(weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mean(weight, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 51.25 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.na(weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(is.na(weight)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ### P1.5.3 Operators {.unnumbered} | Operator | Meaning | |---|---| | `<-` | assignment | | `+ - * / ^` | arithmetic | | `== != < > <= >=` | comparison | | & | ! | logical *and*, *or*, *not* | | `%in%` | membership, e.g. `sex %in% c("female")` | | `$` | extraction of a column from a data frame | | |> | pipe: passes the result on the left to the function on the right | ## P1.6 Functions and packages {.unnumbered} A **function** takes inputs (*arguments*) and returns an output. Arguments can be given by position or by name; arguments with default values can be omitted. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} round(123.456, digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 123.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 0 5 10 15 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rep("A", times = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "A" "A" "A" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} paste("District", 1:3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "District 1" "District 2" "District 3" ``` ::: ::: Additional functions are provided by **packages**. A package is installed once with `install.packages("name")` and loaded in each session with `library(name)`. The help page of a function is displayed with `?function_name`, e.g. `?seq`. ### P1.6.1 Writing functions {.unnumbered} User-defined functions avoid repeating code: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} incidence_per_100k <- function(cases, population) { cases / population * 100000 } incidence_per_100k(cases = 375, population = 250000) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 150 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} incidence_per_100k(cases = c(10, 50, 120), population = c(20000, 80000, 150000)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 50.0 62.5 80.0 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.7 Conditional statements and loops {.unnumbered} `if` executes code only when a condition is true; `ifelse()` applies a condition to every element of a vector. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} coverage <- 0.82 if (coverage >= 0.95) { message("Coverage target reached") } else { message("Coverage below target") } ifelse(age >= 15, "adult", "child") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "child" "child" "adult" "adult" "adult" ``` ::: ::: A `for` loop repeats a block of code for each value of a sequence: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} savings <- numeric(5) # empty vector of length 5 savings[1] <- 100 for (year in 2:5) { savings[year] <- savings[year - 1] * 1.10 # 10% interest per year } savings ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 100.00 110.00 121.00 133.10 146.41 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.8 Lists {.unnumbered} A **list** can contain objects of different types and lengths, and is often used to store parameters or the results of an analysis. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} parameters <- list(country = "Mozambique", year = 2026, rates = c(0.1, 0.25)) parameters$country ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] "Mozambique" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} parameters[["rates"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 0.10 0.25 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.9 Data frames {.unnumbered} A **data frame** is a table in which each column is a vector and each row an observation. A `tibble` is the `tidyverse` version of a data frame. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) patients <- tibble( id = 1:5, age = age, sex = sex, vaccinated = vaccinated, visit = visit ) patients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 5 × 5 ## id age sex vaccinated visit ## ## 1 1 4 female TRUE 2026-03-01 ## 2 2 12 male FALSE 2026-03-04 ## 3 3 35 male TRUE 2026-03-04 ## 4 4 67 female TRUE 2026-03-09 ## 5 5 23 female FALSE 2026-03-12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} patients$age # one column ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4 12 35 67 23 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(patients); ncol(patients) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(patients$age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. ## 4.0 12.0 23.0 28.2 35.0 67.0 ``` ::: ::: ### P1.9.1 Data manipulation with dplyr {.unnumbered} The principal functions of the `dplyr` package each perform one operation and are combined with the pipe `|>`: | Function | Operation | |---|---| | `filter()` | select rows | | `select()` | select columns | | `mutate()` | create or modify columns | | `arrange()` | sort rows | | `group_by()` and `summarise()` | summarise by group | | `count()` | count rows by group | | `left_join()` | combine two tables by a common column | ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} patients |> filter(age >= 15) |> mutate(age_months = age * 12) |> select(id, sex, age, age_months) |> arrange(desc(age)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 3 × 4 ## id sex age age_months ## ## 1 4 female 67 804 ## 2 3 male 35 420 ## 3 5 female 23 276 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} patients |> group_by(sex) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age), prop_vaccinated = mean(vaccinated)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 2 × 4 ## sex n mean_age prop_vaccinated ## ## 1 female 3 31.3 0.667 ## 2 male 2 23.5 0.5 ``` ::: ::: ### P1.9.2 Long and wide formats {.unnumbered} Data in **wide** format have one column per variable or time point; data in **long** format have one row per observation and a column identifying the variable. Long format is required by `ggplot2`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} wide <- tibble(district = c("A", "B"), `2024` = c(120, 85), `2025` = c(140, 60)) long <- wide |> pivot_longer(-district, names_to = "year", values_to = "cases") long ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 4 × 3 ## district year cases ## ## 1 A 2024 120 ## 2 A 2025 140 ## 3 B 2024 85 ## 4 B 2025 60 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} long |> pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = cases) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 2 × 3 ## district `2024` `2025` ## ## 1 A 120 140 ## 2 B 85 60 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.10 Importing and exporting data {.unnumbered} The code below illustrates the import and export of files. The names `my_data.csv`, `my_data.xlsx` and `my_data_clean.csv` are hypothetical examples, to be replaced by the names of actual data files stored in the `data/` folder of the project. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # "my_data" is a placeholder: replace it with the name of your own file library(readr) data <- read_csv("data/my_data.csv") # text files with comma-separated values library(readxl) data <- read_excel("data/my_data.xlsx") # Excel files write_csv(data, "output/my_data_clean.csv") # export ``` ::: After importing a dataset, it should be inspected with `head()`, `glimpse()`, `summary()` and `View()`. ## P1.11 Graphs with ggplot2 {.unnumbered} A `ggplot2` graph is constructed from three components: a data frame, an **aesthetic mapping** of variables to visual properties with `aes()`, and one or more **geometries** (`geom_point()`, `geom_line()`, `geom_col()`, `geom_histogram()`, etc.). Labels are added with `labs()` and panels with `facet_wrap()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(long, aes(x = year, y = cases, fill = district)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of cases", fill = "District") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](00a-prelim-r.fr_files/figure-docx/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} growth <- tibble(day = 0:30, children = 50 * 1.08^(0:30), adults = 30 * 1.05^(0:30)) |> pivot_longer(-day, names_to = "group", values_to = "cases") ggplot(growth, aes(day, cases, colour = group)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + labs(x = "Day", y = "Cases", colour = "Age group") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](00a-prelim-r.fr_files/figure-docx/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## P1.12 Random numbers {.unnumbered} R generates random numbers from many probability distributions, for example `runif()` (uniform), `rnorm()` (normal), `rbinom()` (binomial) and `rpois()` (Poisson). `set.seed()` makes the results reproducible. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2027) rnorm(3, mean = 0, sd = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] -0.9348780 -0.6938629 -0.5479451 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rbinom(5, size = 10, prob = 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4 2 6 5 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sample(1:6, size = 4, replace = TRUE) # four throws of a die ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 4 1 6 4 ``` ::: ::: ## P1.13 Errors and help {.unnumbered} Error messages indicate where execution failed. Common causes include misspelled object names (`object 'x' not found`), packages that have not been loaded (`could not find function`), unmatched brackets or quotes, and code executed in the wrong order. Further help is available from the help pages (`?function`), the package documentation (reference manuals and vignettes on CRAN, ), the [Epidemiologist R Handbook](https://www.epirhandbook.com) and online forums such as [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/r) and [Posit Community](https://forum.posit.co). AI assistants can explain error messages and suggest code, but their suggestions must be checked and understood before use. ::: {.callout-tip icon="false"} ## Exercise 1. Create a vector with the weekly numbers of cases 3, 7, 12, 25, 31 and 28. Calculate the total, the mean and the week with the highest number of cases. 2. Write a function `percent_change(old, new)` that returns the percentage change between two values, and apply it to consecutive weeks of the vector above (hint: `x[-1]` and `x[-length(x)]`). 3. Using the `patients` data frame, calculate the proportion vaccinated among children and adults. 4. Create a data frame with two columns, `week` (1–6) and `cases` (the vector of question 1), and plot the cases as a bar chart. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(3, 7, 12, 25, 31, 28) c(total = sum(x), mean = mean(x), peak_week = which.max(x)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## total mean peak_week ## 106.00000 17.66667 5.00000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} percent_change <- function(old, new) (new - old) / old * 100 round(percent_change(x[-length(x)], x[-1]), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## [1] 133.3 71.4 108.3 24.0 -9.7 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} patients |> mutate(group = ifelse(age >= 15, "adult", "child")) |> group_by(group) |> summarise(prop_vaccinated = mean(vaccinated)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ## # A tibble: 2 × 2 ## group prop_vaccinated ## ## 1 adult 0.667 ## 2 child 0.5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(week = 1:6, cases = x) |> ggplot(aes(week, cases)) + geom_col(fill = "steelblue") + labs(x = "Week", y = "Cases") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](00a-prelim-r.fr_files/figure-docx/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ::: ## P1.14 Self-assessment {.unnumbered .keep-short} Participants should be able to perform the following tasks without assistance before the first module: - [ ] Create an RStudio Project, open a script and execute it line by line. - [ ] Install and load a package, and consult the help page of a function. - [ ] Create vectors of different types, select elements and handle missing values. - [ ] Write a function with two arguments. - [ ] Import a CSV file and inspect it with `head()`, `glimpse()` and `summary()`. - [ ] Use `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()` and `summarise()`. - [ ] Convert a table between wide and long formats. - [ ] Produce a bar chart and a line graph with `ggplot2`. - [ ] Write an `if` statement and a `for` loop. ## P1.15 Additional resources {.unnumbered .keep-short} - **Applied Epi interactive R tutorials** (English, French, Portuguese, Spanish): . - **The Epidemiologist R Handbook** (available in several languages): — in particular the chapters on R basics, data cleaning, dates, grouping and `ggplot2`. - **R for Data Science**, 2nd edition (Wickham H., Çetinkaya-Rundel M., Grolemund G.): . - **Hands-On Programming with R** (Grolemund G.): — objects, functions and loops. - **PATH/MACEPA Data Fellowship materials**, developed for public health staff in Africa and based on routine (DHIS2-type) malaria data; overview at : - *Foundational R Skills* (): R and RStudio, `dplyr`/`tidyr`, `ggplot2`, messy data and joins; - *Secondary Topics for Data Analysis in R* (): functions, loops, error messages, maps, data completeness and time series plots; - *Foundational Data Skills* (): organisation of project folders, version control with Git and GitHub. - **AMMnet Hackathon live sessions** (Applied Malaria Modeling Network), with recordings, code and data: — data visualisation, data wrangling and mapping in R, some sessions in French and Portuguese.
